summary.text: Take the composite number \(n=23492890653051=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341\). The gcd-sum is multiplicative and has value \(2p-1\) at a prime \(p\), so here it equals \(610815156979325\), whose successor is \(26n\); thus the relevant gcd is \(n\) and the resulting quotient is \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
G(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n)
\]
and
\[
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+G(n))}.
\]
We will exhibit a composite positive integer \(N\neq 1\) for which \(a(N)=1\).

The counterexample is
\[
N=23492890653051=3\cdot 37\cdot 43\cdot 42307\cdot 116341.
\]
We first establish the formula that will make it possible to evaluate the very large gcd-sum without adding its terms individually.

For every positive integer \(n\), partition the integers \(k\) with \(1\leq k\leq n\) according to the value \(d=\gcd(k,n)\). Such a value \(d\) must divide \(n\). For a fixed divisor \(d\mid n\), writing \(k=dj\) gives
\[
\gcd(k,n)=d \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \gcd(j,n/d)=1,
\]
where \(1\leq j\leq n/d\). There are exactly \(\varphi(n/d)\) such integers \(j\), where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function. This statement includes the case \(d=n\): then \(n/d=1\), and the single value \(j=1\) is counted by \(\varphi(1)=1\). Every member of the class belonging to \(d\) contributes \(d\) to the gcd-sum. Therefore
\[
G(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d). \tag{1}
\]

The function \(G\) is multiplicative. Indeed, suppose \(m\) and \(n\) are coprime. Every divisor of \(mn\) can be written uniquely as \(d_1d_2\), with \(d_1\mid m\) and \(d_2\mid n\). Moreover, \(m/d_1\) and \(n/d_2\) are coprime. Euler's totient is multiplicative on coprime arguments (this follows, for example, from the Chinese remainder correspondence between reduced residue classes modulo \(m_1m_2\) and pairs of reduced residue classes modulo coprime \(m_1,m_2\)). Applying (1), we consequently obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(mn)
&=\sum_{d_1\mid m}\sum_{d_2\mid n}
 d_1d_2\,\varphi\!\left(\frac{m}{d_1}\frac{n}{d_2}\right)\\
&=\sum_{d_1\mid m}\sum_{d_2\mid n}
 d_1d_2\,\varphi(m/d_1)\varphi(n/d_2)\\
&=\left(\sum_{d_1\mid m}d_1\varphi(m/d_1)\right)
  \left(\sum_{d_2\mid n}d_2\varphi(n/d_2)\right)\\
&=G(m)G(n). \tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(p\) is prime, its only divisors are \(1\) and \(p\). Formula (1), together with \(\varphi(p)=p-1\) and \(\varphi(1)=1\), gives
\[
G(p)=\varphi(p)+p\varphi(1)=(p-1)+p=2p-1. \tag{3}
\]

For completeness, we now justify that all five displayed factors of \(N\) are prime. The primality of \(3,37,43\) follows immediately by trial division: for \(37\) one need only test the primes \(2,3,5\), and for \(43\) one need only test \(2,3,5\); none divides the relevant number.

We use the following elementary \(n-1\) criterion for the two larger factors. Suppose that \(M>1\), that the complete prime factorization of \(M-1\) is known, and that there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{M-1}\equiv1\pmod M
\]
and, for every distinct prime \(q\mid M-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(M-1)/q}-1,M\bigr)=1. \tag{4}
\]
Then \(M\) is prime. To see this, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(M\). The first congruence implies that \(b\) is coprime to \(r\), so its multiplicative order modulo \(r\) is defined and divides \(M-1\). Condition (4) says that this order does not divide \((M-1)/q\) for any prime \(q\mid M-1\). Hence the order contains the full prime-power contribution of every prime in \(M-1\), and therefore the order is exactly \(M-1\). On the other hand, the order divides \(r-1\). Thus \(M-1\mid r-1\), so \(r\geq M\). Since \(r\mid M\), this forces \(r=M\), proving that \(M\) is prime.

For \(M=42307\), we have the complete factorization
\[
M-1=42306=2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot641.
\]
The number \(641\) is prime: its square root is less than \(26\), and its remainders upon division by the primes \(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\) are respectively
\[
1,2,1,4,3,4,12,14,20,
\]
all nonzero. Taking \(b=3\), modular exponentiation gives
\[
3^{42306}\equiv1\pmod{42307},
\]
and the data for the four distinct prime divisors of \(42306\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
q&(42306)/q&3^{42306/q}\bmod 42307&
\gcd(3^{42306/q}-1,42307)\\ \hline
2&21153&42306&1\\
3&14102&36715&1\\
11&3846&17937&1\\
641&66&10961&1
\end{array}
\]
(The modular residues are obtained by ordinary repeated squaring; the last column is obtained by the Euclidean algorithm.) Thus the criterion proves that \(42307\) is prime.

For \(M=116341\), the complete factorization is
\[
M-1=116340=2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277.
\]
The number \(277\) is prime: its square root is less than \(17\), and its remainders modulo \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) are respectively
\[
1,1,2,4,2,4,
\]
so it has no prime divisor at most its square root. Taking \(b=14\), modular exponentiation gives
\[
14^{116340}\equiv1\pmod{116341},
\]
and for the distinct prime divisors of \(116340\) we obtain
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
q&(116340)/q&14^{116340/q}\bmod 116341&
\gcd(14^{116340/q}-1,116341)\\ \hline
2&58170&116340&1\\
3&38780&50801&1\\
5&23268&81650&1\\
7&16620&10889&1\\
277&420&35125&1
\end{array}
\]
Again, repeated squaring gives the third column and the Euclidean algorithm gives the fourth. The criterion therefore proves that \(116341\) is prime.

Thus the five factors
\[
3,\quad37,\quad43,\quad42307,\quad116341
\]
are distinct primes, and in particular are pairwise coprime. Their product can be checked in stages:
\[
3\cdot37=111,
\qquad111\cdot43=4773,
\]
\[
4773\cdot42307=201931311,
\]
and
\[
201931311\cdot116341=23492890653051=N.
\]
By multiplicativity (2) and the prime evaluation (3),
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(N)
&=(2\cdot3-1)(2\cdot37-1)(2\cdot43-1)
  (2\cdot42307-1)(2\cdot116341-1)\\
&=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681.
\end{aligned}
\]
The product is again conveniently checked in stages:
\[
5\cdot73=365,
\qquad365\cdot85=31025,
\]
\[
31025\cdot84613=2625118325,
\]
and
\[
2625118325\cdot232681=610815156979325.
\]
Consequently
\[
G(N)=610815156979325.
\]
The crucial divisibility is the exact equality
\[
1+G(N)=610815156979326
       =26\cdot23492890653051
       =26N. \tag{5}
\]
It follows from (5) that
\[
\gcd(N,1+G(N))=\gcd(N,26N)=N.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(N)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,1+G(N))}=\frac{N}{N}=1.
\]

Finally, \(N\neq1\), and \(N\) is not prime: the displayed factorization shows, for example, that \(3\mid N\) while \(N>3\). Hence \(N\) is a composite integer for which \(a(N)=1\). This contradicts the claimed implication that \(a(n)=1\) only when \(n=1\) or \(n\) is prime, and therefore disproves the conjectured equivalence.
